lessons.title: SEBI's Algo Trading Framework — Approval, Tagging, and Kill Switches

children.text: A strategy that trades faster than a human can react is also a strategy that can go wrong faster than a human can react. SEBI's algorithmic trading framework exists almost entirely to make sure someone, and something automated, can stop that before it becomes a real problem.
You Can't Just Turn On an Algo

Running an algorithmic trading strategy on an Indian exchange is not simply a matter of writing code and connecting to an order gateway. Exchanges require an algorithmic strategy to be tested and approved before it can go live, and that approval is what makes the algo ID field from the previous chapter meaningful in the first place: it is not just a label, it is proof that a specific strategy has actually been through the approval process before it is allowed to send a single order.

body.caption: Two broad categories of algo trading oversight

cells: Exchange approval of the strategy, ongoing surveillance of its order flow
Retail traders using a broker's trading API
Broker-level responsibility for client algos, plus SEBI's evolving rules for API-based retail trading

children.text: Every Order Has to Point Back to an Approved Strategy

The algo ID covered in the previous chapter is the mechanism that makes this approval process enforceable rather than theoretical. Every algorithmic order carries that ID, which means an exchange's surveillance systems can, at any moment, trace any single order back to a specific approved strategy, and by extension back to whichever desk or client is running it. This is precisely the same principle Chapter 3's lesson on clock synchronization relied on: an audit trail is only useful if every piece of it, timestamp and now strategy identity, is trustworthy and complete.

body.label: Core Requirement
body.value: Every algo order must carry an approved, unique strategy ID
body.context: This is what lets an exchange's surveillance system trace any order back to a specific approved strategy, rather than treating algo flow as an anonymous stream.

children.text: The Kill Switch: A Regulatory Requirement, Not Just Good Practice

markDefs.definition: A control that lets a broker, trading member, or exchange immediately halt trading and cancel outstanding orders for a specific algorithm, dealer, or client, used to contain a malfunctioning or runaway strategy.

children.text: Both exchange members and, in some cases, the exchange itself are required to maintain a

: a mechanism that can immediately halt trading and cancel outstanding orders for a specific algo, dealer, or client, the moment something looks wrong. This is not an optional safety feature a careful firm might choose to build. It is a baseline regulatory expectation, precisely because a malfunctioning algorithm can generate more damage in the time it takes a human to notice than almost any other kind of trading error.

body.title: The 3 a.m. Bug
body.scenario: A firm's algorithm has a bug: instead of sending one order in response to a price move, it enters a loop and sends the same order repeatedly, hundreds of times within a few seconds, before anyone notices the strategy is malfunctioning.
body.prompt: What is supposed to stop this from turning into a much bigger problem, and what should happen once it is noticed?
body.modelAnswer: The firm's kill switch is what is supposed to contain this: either an automated risk control that detects the abnormal order rate and halts the algo itself, or a manual kill switch a risk manager or dealer triggers the moment the runaway behaviour is noticed, immediately stopping new orders and cancelling whatever is still outstanding. Once triggered, the firm should not simply restart the strategy. It needs to investigate the root cause of the bug, since the algo ID tagging covered earlier means the exchange's surveillance systems will already have flagged this exact strategy, and restarting a known-faulty algo without fixing it first invites both further losses and regulatory scrutiny.

body.text: The framework described above reflects the general shape of SEBI's algorithmic trading regulation: strategy approval, unique ID tagging, and mandatory kill switch controls. SEBI's specific requirements, including the treatment of retail API-based algo trading, have been revised more than once in recent years. Check SEBI's current circulars for the exact, up-to-date requirements before relying on any specific detail here for compliance purposes.
Speed without a kill switch is not an edge. It is just a faster way to find out how bad a bug can get before anyone can stop it.

points: Algorithmic strategies on Indian exchanges typically require exchange approval before going live, and the algo ID tagging covered in the previous chapter is what makes that approval enforceable order by order.
Institutional and colocated algos are typically overseen through exchange approval and surveillance, while retail API-based algo trading has its own, separately evolving layer of SEBI oversight.
A kill switch, the ability to immediately halt trading and cancel outstanding orders for a specific algo, dealer, or client, is a baseline regulatory expectation, not an optional safety feature.
Treat the specifics of SEBI's current algo trading rules as something to verify directly against its published circulars, since this area has been revised multiple times in recent years.
